title: "You've Been Doing This Wrong" Myth-Buster Hook
whatYouGet: A myth-busting short that corrects a common math mistake with proof.
howToUse: Name the common mistake; the AI builds the wrong-vs-right reveal short.
effectiveUsage: 1. Open any free AI chat.
2. Paste the prompt and the mistake.
3. State class level.
4. Record the wrong-then-right reveal.
5. Ask for a softer tone if too harsh.
commonFix: If the correction is unclear, reply: "Show the wrong method and the right method side by side with the same numbers and verify the right answer."
promptText:
ROLE: Act as a myth-busting maths content writer who corrects common student errors with proof.

CONTEXT: This is a 30 to 50 second vertical short for [CLASS/GRADE] students of [BOARD or EXAM e.g. CBSE / ICSE / State Board / JEE / NEET]. The hook is the classic "you have been doing this wrong" pattern: name a common mistake, show why it is wrong, then teach the correct way. Spoken to camera.

YOUR TASK:
1. Take the common mistake I give and open with a confident "you have been doing this wrong" style hook (give 3 hook options).
2. Show the WRONG method on a sample problem and the wrong answer it produces.
3. Show the RIGHT method on the SAME problem and the correct answer.
4. Explain in one line WHY the wrong method fails.
5. End with a memorable correction the student will not forget.

INPUT: Here is the common mistake and level: [PASTE THE MISTAKE AND CLASS LEVEL HERE].

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Work both the wrong and right methods fully on the same numbers. VERIFY the correct answer by two independent methods. Never misrepresent the wrong method as a straw man; show the real mistake students actually make. Keep all maths legible in plain text or LaTeX.

OUTPUT FORMAT (in this order):
HOOK OPTIONS: 3 spoken lines.
THE WRONG WAY (5-20s): spoken + on-screen maths in [BRACKETS], ending in the wrong answer.
THE RIGHT WAY (20-40s): spoken + on-screen maths in [BRACKETS], ending in the correct answer.
WHY IT FAILS: one line.
REMEMBER (40-50s): the memorable correction.
ON-SCREEN TEXT: 4 caption phrases.
VERIFICATION NOTE: how the correct answer was checked two ways.

RULES: Be firm but kind, never mocking. Same numbers in both methods. Under 120 spoken words. Flawless, legible maths.

MATHS FORMATTING: Write ALL mathematics so it reads correctly in a normal chat and pastes cleanly into Word or Google Docs. Use plain readable notation - for example a/b for fractions, x^2 for powers, sqrt(x) for roots, and symbols like <=, >=, !=, +-, pi, theta, integral and sum. Do NOT output raw LaTeX or code such as \frac{}{}, \sqrt{}, x^{2}, $...$ or \( ... \) - these appear as broken symbols to a teacher in a free chat.
Footer: At the very end add a footer line: "Prepared by [YOUR NAME]", and put "Compiled by [YOUR NAME]" in the header block.

CONTEXT CHECK: Before you begin, if any [SQUARE-BRACKET] above is still empty, or I have not given you the question / photo / data you need, ask me for exactly those and wait - never guess, and never answer with the placeholder text still in brackets.

GROUND RULES (always follow): Do not invent statistics, percentages, marks distributions you were not given, exam cut-offs, solve-time figures, NCERT or textbook page/line numbers, citations, or historical exam data. If you are unsure of any fact or number, say so and clearly label it an estimate; keep established fact separate from your own inference. Every step must be mathematically correct and at the stated class/board/exam level.

promptText:
ROLE: Act as a social media caption writer who specialises in education accounts for mathematics teachers.

CONTEXT: I run a teaching page on Instagram for [CLASS/GRADE] students preparing for [BOARD or EXAM e.g. CBSE / JEE / NEET / State Board]. I want captions that sound human and warm, not robotic, and that make people stop, read, and save.

2. Caption A: short and punchy (under 40 words).
3. Caption B: a relatable story or struggle that ends with the lesson.
4. Caption C: a question-led caption that invites comments.
5. Each caption must end with a clear, friendly call to action.
6. Then give one clean hashtag block.

INPUT: Here is what my post shows: [PASTE A SHORT DESCRIPTION, e.g. a carousel on solving quadratic equations by factoring]. My city or region is: [PASTE, e.g. Patna / Delhi / Hyderabad] (use this only to add a couple of local-reach hashtags).

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Do not invent fake statistics, fake student quotes, or fake results. If you mention a maths fact in a caption, verify it is correct before writing it. Keep every claim honest and checkable. Keep all text in clean plain language with straight quotes only.

OUTPUT FORMAT: Use this exact structure.
CAPTION A (Short): ...
CAPTION B (Story): ...
CAPTION C (Question): ...
